target_claim: The reduction (conflict graph G unchanged, ferry capacity k = c+1) makes river-crossing feasibility equivalent to c-colorability; in particular, if G is c-colorable then a valid crossing sequence exists.
source_quote:
**Part 1: G is c-colorable ⇒Valid crossing sequence exists.** - Let C1, C2, . . . , Cc be
the color classes (independent sets) of G. - **Crossing Strategy**: 1. Charon takes all
passengers in C1 to the other side (since |C1| ≤c, this fits within capacity k = c + 1).
2. Charon returns alone. 3. Repeat for each color class C2, . . . , Cc.
test_sketch: Implement the reduction (trivial: instance -> (G, k=c+1)) plus a brute-force oracle: BFS over states (set of passengers on left bank, Charon side), moves = Charon crossing with any subset of <= k-1 passengers from his bank, a state is legal iff each Charon-free bank induces an independent set of G; accept iff (empty set, Charon right) reachable. Compare against a brute-force c-coloring check on all graphs with n <= 8 and c in {2,3}. Failing input: G = two disjoint triangles, c = 3, so k = 4. G is 3-colorable, but any first departure leaves >= 3 passengers on the left bank without Charon while the maximum independent set of 2K3 has size 2, so every first move is unsafe and the oracle reports NO valid crossing sequence - refuting the claimed 'c-colorable => valid sequence' direction and the iff. The solution's stated invariant (lines 0034-0035, 'the remaining passengers are in independent sets') is also directly false since the remainder is a union of color classes.
